analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $15, then $20, with automatic raises tied to median wage growth.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2026 with no cosponsors and referred to committee, where it has received no action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to raise the federal minimum wage in steps: $15 an hour starting January 1, 2027, $17.50 in 2028, and $20 in 2029. After that, the wage would rise automatically each year based on growth in the median hourly wage, so it would no longer lose value to inflation while Congress does nothing. The bill was introduced by Rep. Norma Torres with no cosponsors and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it has sat with no action.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the roughly 20-30 million workers earning near the federal minimum wage would see raises in three steps to $20 an hour by 2029, with automatic annual increases afterward tied to median wage growth so the floor keeps pace with typical pay. Workers in the many states still at or near the $7.25 federal floor would gain the most.

how_it_helps.text: It raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $15 an hour on January 1, 2027, then to $17.50 in 2028 and $20 in 2029.
From 2030 onward, the wage rises automatically each year with the growth in the median hourly wage, so it would no longer lose value while Congress sits idle.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay low wages — especially retail, restaurants, and other labor-intensive businesses — would bear higher payroll costs, and some of that cost would likely be passed to consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: The step to $20 an hour by 2029 roughly doubles the current federal floor over four years, a pace that would raise labor costs sharply for small businesses and low-margin employers in lower-cost regions, with no small-business exception or regional adjustment in the bill text.

Opponents of minimum wage increases generally argue that large mandated raises can reduce entry-level hiring or push prices up; the bill text includes no study or phased flexibility to address those concerns.
The bill has no cosponsors, indicating no visible cross-party or even intra-party coalition behind it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would be substantial for low-wage workers — a raise to $20 an hour plus automatic raises tied to median wage growth, which ends the cycle of Congress letting the minimum wage erode for decades. The main costs fall on employers paying low wages, especially small businesses and labor-intensive sectors, and some economists would warn of reduced hiring or higher prices, though the bill contains no small-business exemptions or phase-in flexibility to soften those costs for the smallest employers. On the record here, the bigger fact is that the bill never received any consideration: no cosponsors and no committee action one day after introduction, in a chamber whose committee majority has not scheduled it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Education and Workforce Committee, where it sits with no cosponsors and no scheduled action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 3, 2026 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.
No committee action, hearing, or floor vote has been recorded since introduction.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-wage employers who would have paid the higher wage are better off so far, since the bill has not advanced; no worker has gained anything yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have paid more

for.name: Rep. Norma Torres
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and is its sole sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; the bill has a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no recorded support or opposition from either party.

industries.industry: Low-wage employers (retail, food service, hospitality, care work)
industries.note: These employers would face steadily rising wage bills, reaching $20 an hour by 2029 and automatic increases after that. Many pay wages at or near the current $7.25 floor, so the increase would be largest for them.

industries.industry: Hourly workers earning near the federal minimum
industries.note: Workers earning under $20 an hour would see directly mandated raises, and the median-wage index would preserve those gains against inflation over time.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is one day old with zero cosponsors and sits in a committee controlled by the opposing party; the overwhelming majority of member bills referred to committee never receive a hearing or a vote, and without cosponsors or committee action early in its life this bill is very unlikely to advance this Congress.
